claims.claim: Listening to the sounds produced within the body, typically using a stethoscope, is called auscultation; the OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing glossary calls it the technique of listening to the sounds produced within the body, MedlinePlus describes auscultation as listening to sounds, usually with a stethoscope, and the Open RN text describes it as listening to sounds such as heart, lung, and bowel sounds created by organs using a stethoscope.

The stethoscope is a piece of medical equipment used to amplify the body's internal sounds; it is mostly used to listen to the heart, lungs, and bowel sounds and is also used to obtain manual blood pressure; a dual-headed stethoscope has a diaphragm (larger, flat) and a bell (smaller, concave), with the bell used for low-frequency sounds such as heart sounds and the diaphragm working best for breath sounds.

Auscultation is one of the four physical exam techniques listed by MedlinePlus (inspection, palpation, auscultation, percussion) and is essential for assessing the function of the heart, lungs, and abdomen.

Heart auscultation is routinely performed over five specific areas of the chest to listen for corresponding valvular sounds; the S1 and S2 sounds make the familiar 'lub-dub' sound, S1 ('lub') corresponds to the palpable pulse and S2 ('dub') marks the end of systole; the nurse identifies S1 and S2 while evaluating rate and rhythm, and an apical heart rate is auscultated for a full minute when accuracy matters.

Auscultation of the lungs involves listening to breath sounds, including inspiratory and expiratory sounds, and any adventitious (unusual) sounds such as crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi; MedlinePlus adds that normal lung sounds occur in all parts of the chest area and that abnormal breath sounds include rales (small clicking, bubbling, or rattling sounds heard on inhalation), rhonchi, stridor, and wheezing.

Correct placement of the stethoscope is important for a quality lung assessment: the chest piece should not be placed over clothes or hair because these create inaccurate sounds from friction; the examiner listens side to side to compare symmetrical lung fields and listens through the entire respiratory cycle because different sounds may be heard on inspiration and expiration.

Normal bowel sounds indicate the presence of peristalsis and normal gastrointestinal motility, while changes in bowel sounds may signify conditions such as bowel obstruction, ileus, or intestinal inflammation; MedlinePlus adds that most bowel sounds are normal and simply mean the gastrointestinal tract is working, and that a provider checks them by listening to the abdomen with a stethoscope.

A heart murmur is a blowing, whooshing, or rasping sound heard during a heartbeat, caused by turbulent blood flow through the heart valves or near the heart; the provider can listen to heart sounds by placing a stethoscope on the chest.

Naming abnormal sounds takes training: extra heart sounds (clicks, murmurs, S3, S4, friction rubs) can be difficult for a novice to distinguish, so if any new or different sounds are noticed the nurse should consult an advanced practitioner or notify the provider; beginner nurses are advised to concentrate first on rate and regularity.

Auscultation findings prompt action rather than making a diagnosis alone: crackles in the lung bases of a heart-failure patient indicate fluid accumulation (Fundamentals of Nursing), and an RN narrative in the thorax chapter describes hearing crackles and limited air movement in a patient later found to have severe pneumonia and calling a rapid response.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The same abnormal lung sound goes by different names across sources: MedlinePlus calls the crackling sound heard on inhalation 'rales,' while the OpenStax texts use 'crackles' and note the equivalence in their own glossary ('fine crackles (rales)') and assessment tables.
positions: MedlinePlus Breath sounds: 'Rales. Small clicking, bubbling, or rattling sounds in the lungs. They are heard when a person breathes in (inhales).'
OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills glossary and chapter 23 tables: 'Fine crackles (rales) — intermittent high-pitched popping or crackling sounds heard on inspiration.'
OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing 12.3 uses 'crackles' (e.g., crackles in the lung bases with heart failure).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'crackles' as its main term (the OpenStax backbone) and names 'rales' once alongside it so a reader meeting either term is not confused. No sound descriptions are quoted from any source.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Guidance on which side of the stethoscope to use differs by context: the equipment section of Clinical Nursing Skills says low-frequency sounds such as heart sounds are heard with the bell and the diaphragm works best for breath sounds, while the cardiac assessment chapter instructs using the diaphragm to identify S1 and S2 and then repeating with the bell.
positions: CNS 15.1 (equipment): bell for low-frequency sounds such as heart sounds; diaphragm best for breath sounds.
CNS 24.3 (cardiac assessment): 'Use the diaphragm of the stethoscope to carefully identify the S1 and S2 sounds... Repeat this process with the bell of the stethoscope.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the equipment guidance (bell for low-frequency heart sounds, diaphragm for breath sounds) and notes that the cardiac assessment uses both sides in sequence — a technique detail, not a contradiction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Normal bowel sounds may be described differently in charting practice: the OpenStax texts document 'bowel sounds present in all four quadrants' as a normal finding, while MedlinePlus notes that hyperactive sounds can sometimes be heard even without a stethoscope (e.g., 'stomach growling') and that hypoactive sounds are normal during sleep.
positions: OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: 'Bowel sounds present in all 4 quadrants' appears as the normal documentation line in the abdomen section.
MedlinePlus Abdominal sounds: 'Most bowel sounds are normal. They simply mean that the gastrointestinal tract is working.'
MedlinePlus Abdominal sounds: 'Hypoactive bowel sounds are normal during sleep.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states simply that most bowel sounds are normal and mean the GI tract is working, and that it is the change from expected sounds — or their absence — that is worth attention.

sourceRecords.title: Physical examination (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: a physical examination usually includes inspection (looking at the body), palpation (feeling the body with fingers or hands), auscultation (listening to sounds, usually with a stethoscope), and percussion (producing sounds, usually by tapping on specific areas of the body). Used to corroborate the working definition of auscultation and to place it among the four exam techniques. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Heart sounds (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: NEW source id (no prior registry entry); verified live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: a heart murmur is a blowing, whooshing, or rasping sound heard during a heartbeat, caused by turbulent (rough) blood flow through the heart valves or near the heart; the provider can listen to heart sounds by placing a stethoscope on the chest; murmurs are graded by loudness and described by the stage of the heartbeat when heard. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Breath sounds (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: NEW source id; verified live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200; article located via the encyclopedia B index, not the retired 003323 id). Supports: breath sounds are the noises produced by the structures of the lungs during breathing; lung sounds are best heard with a stethoscope (auscultation); normal lung sounds occur in all parts of the chest area, including above the collarbones and at the bottom of the rib cage; the four most common abnormal breath sounds are rales (small clicking, bubbling, or rattling sounds heard on inhalation), rhonchi (snoring-like), stridor, and wheezing (high-pitched, narrowed airways, often on exhalation). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Abdominal sounds (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: NEW source id; verified live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200; article located via the encyclopedia A index). Supports: abdominal sounds are the noises made by the intestines; bowel sounds are made by the movement of the intestines as they push food through; the intestines are hollow, so bowel sounds echo through the abdomen much like the sounds heard from water pipes; most bowel sounds are normal and simply mean the gastrointestinal tract is working; a provider checks abdominal sounds by listening to the abdomen with a stethoscope (auscultation); hyperactive and hypoactive bowel sounds described. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Clinical Nursing Skills, Section 24.3: Nursing Assessment (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (per this subject's source-map). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: auscultation is the process of using a stethoscope to listen for normal and abnormal sounds (e.g., components of the heartbeat, murmurs, valvular sounds, bruits); heart auscultation is routinely performed over five specific areas (APE To Man); use the diaphragm to identify S1 and S2, which make a 'lub-dub' sound; S1 ('lub') corresponds to the palpable pulse and S2 ('dub') identifies the end of systole; repeat with the bell; extra heart sounds (clicks, murmurs, S3, S4, friction rubs) can be difficult for a novice to distinguish, so any new or different sounds should be reported by consulting an advanced practitioner or notifying the provider; beginner nurses should concentrate on rate and regularity; the apical pulse is auscultated for a full minute when accuracy matters; auscultation yields more accurate results than percussion and is easier to conduct. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Clinical Nursing Skills, Section 15.1: Performing a General Survey (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (verified OER). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports the stethoscope equipment description: the stethoscope is a piece of medical equipment used to amplify the body's internal sounds to its user; it is mostly used to listen to the heart, lungs, and bowel sounds, and is also used to obtain manual blood pressure; a dual-headed stethoscope consists of a diaphragm (larger, flat circle) and a bell (smaller, concave-shaped piece); for low-frequency sounds such as heart sounds the bell is placed against the skin, and for breath sounds the diaphragm works best. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (verified OER). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: a focused thorax and respiratory objective assessment includes auscultation of lung sounds using a stethoscope; the RN narrative of a patient with severe pneumonia describes using the stethoscope to auscultate the lungs and hearing crackles and limited air movement, then calling a rapid response — used as the real-world example that auscultation findings prompt action. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Clinical Nursing Skills, Section 23.3: Breath Sounds and Lung Assessment (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: NEW source id (no prior registry entry); verified live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200) and via the official book PDF. Supports: correct placement of the stethoscope is important for a quality lung assessment; the stethoscope should not be placed over clothes or hair because these create inaccurate sounds from friction; the best position is the patient sitting upright (or turned side to side if too ill); listen side to side rather than down one side and then the other, to compare symmetrical lung fields; using the diaphragm, listen to the movement of air during inspiration and expiration and listen through the entire respiratory cycle because different sounds may be heard on inspiration and expiration; adventitious sounds include fine or coarse crackles, rhonchi, wheezes, stridor, and friction rubs (the glossary lists fine crackles (rales)). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
